4. Basis, Coordinates, Change-of-Basis Matrix, Matrix Transpose

Author

Zakhar Podyakov

Published

September 23, 2025

Quiz | Flashcards

1. Summary

1.1 Basis of a Vector Space

A basis of a vector space is a fundamental concept in linear algebra. Think of it as a set of building blocks or a coordinate system for that space. For a set of vectors to be a basis, it must satisfy two crucial conditions:

  1. Linearly Independent: None of the vectors in the set can be written as a linear combination of the others. This means each vector adds a unique direction, and there is no redundancy. Imagine three arrows in a 2D plane (like a sheet of paper); one of them is always unnecessary because you can form it from the other two. A basis for a 2D plane will have exactly two such independent arrows.
  2. Spans the Space: Every vector in the entire vector space can be created by taking a specific linear combination of the basis vectors. This ensures that the basis is “complete” and can reach any point in the space.

A common example is the standard basis for \(\mathbb{R}^2\), which consists of two vectors: \[ \mathcal{S} = \left\{ \vec{e}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \vec{e}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \right\} \] Here, \(\vec{e}_1\) is a unit vector along the x-axis, and \(\vec{e}_2\) is a unit vector along the y-axis. Any vector \(\begin{pmatrix} a \\ b \end{pmatrix}\) can be uniquely written as \(a\vec{e}_1 + b\vec{e}_2\).

1.2 Coordinates Relative to a Basis

While a vector is a geometric object (like an arrow), its representation depends on the chosen basis. The coordinate vector of a vector \(\vec{v}\) relative to a basis \(\mathcal{B} = \{\vec{b}_1, \vec{b}_2, \dots, \vec{b}_n\}\) is the unique set of scalars (weights) \(c_1, c_2, \dots, c_n\) such that: \[ \vec{v} = c_1\vec{b}_1 + c_2\vec{b}_2 + \dots + c_n\vec{b}_n \] This set of scalars is written as a column vector and denoted by \([\vec{v}]_{\mathcal{B}}\): \[ [\vec{v}]_{\mathcal{B}} = \begin{pmatrix} c_1 \\ c_2 \\ \vdots \\ c_n \end{pmatrix} \] The key idea is that the same geometric vector will have different coordinate representations in different bases. Changing the basis is like changing the grid system on which you measure the vector’s position.

1.3 Change-of-Basis Matrix
1.3.1 Definition and Purpose

A change-of-basis matrix is a special matrix that systematically converts the coordinates of a vector from one basis to another. The matrix that changes coordinates from a basis \(\mathcal{B}\) (the “old” basis) to a basis \(\mathcal{C}\) (the “new” basis) is denoted \(P_{\mathcal{C} \leftarrow \mathcal{B}}\).

Its job is to perform the following transformation: \[ [\vec{v}]_{\mathcal{C}} = P_{\mathcal{C} \leftarrow \mathcal{B}} [\vec{v}]_{\mathcal{B}} \] To construct this matrix, its columns are the coordinate vectors of the old basis vectors (\(\mathcal{B}\)) written relative to the new basis (\(\mathcal{C}\)). \[ P_{\mathcal{C} \leftarrow \mathcal{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} [\vec{b}_1]_{\mathcal{C}} & [\vec{b}_2]_{\mathcal{C}} & \dots & [\vec{b}_n]_{\mathcal{C}} \end{bmatrix} \]

1.3.2 Changing to the Standard Basis

The process becomes much simpler when converting from a basis \(\mathcal{B} = \{\vec{b}_1, \vec{b}_2, \dots, \vec{b}_n\}\) to the standard basis \(\mathcal{S}\). Since the basis vectors \(\vec{b}_i\) are already expressed in standard coordinates, the change-of-basis matrix \(P_{\mathcal{S} \leftarrow \mathcal{B}}\) is simply the matrix whose columns are the vectors of basis \(\mathcal{B}\). \[ P_{\mathcal{S} \leftarrow \mathcal{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} \vec{b}_1 & \vec{b}_2 & \dots & \vec{b}_n \end{bmatrix} \]

1.3.3 Inverting the Change-of-Basis Matrix

To reverse the process and convert coordinates from basis \(\mathcal{C}\) back to basis \(\mathcal{B}\), you need the inverse of the change-of-basis matrix. \[ P_{\mathcal{B} \leftarrow \mathcal{C}} = (P_{\mathcal{C} \leftarrow \mathcal{B}})^{-1} \] This gives the transformation: \[ [\vec{v}]_{\mathcal{B}} = P_{\mathcal{B} \leftarrow \mathcal{C}} [\vec{v}]_{\mathcal{C}} \]

1.4 The Transpose of a Matrix
1.4.1 Definition

The transpose of a matrix \(A\), denoted \(A^T\), is the matrix obtained by flipping the matrix over its main diagonal. This operation swaps the rows and columns. If \(A\) is an \(m \times n\) matrix, then \(A^T\) will be an \(n \times m\) matrix. The element at position \((i, j)\) in \(A\) moves to position \((j, i)\) in \(A^T\).

For example: If \(A = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \\ e & f \end{pmatrix}\), then \(A^T = \begin{pmatrix} a & c & e \\ b & d & f \end{pmatrix}\).

1.4.2 Properties of the Transpose

The transpose operation has several useful properties:

  • Double Transpose: Taking the transpose twice returns the original matrix: \((A^T)^T = A\).
  • Transpose of a Sum: The transpose of a sum of matrices is the sum of their transposes: \((A + B)^T = A^T + B^T\).
  • Transpose of a Scalar Multiple: A scalar can be factored out of a transpose operation: \((\lambda A)^T = \lambda A^T\).

2. Definitions

  • Basis: A set of linearly independent vectors that spans a vector space.
  • Linearly Independent: A set of vectors where no vector can be expressed as a linear combination of the others.
  • Spanning Set: A set of vectors from which every vector in the space can be created through a linear combination.
  • Coordinate Vector: The column vector of scalars (coefficients) that represents a vector as a linear combination of basis vectors. Its notation is \([\vec{v}]_{\mathcal{B}}\).
  • Change-of-Basis Matrix: A matrix, denoted \(P_{\mathcal{C} \leftarrow \mathcal{B}}\), that transforms coordinate vectors from basis \(\mathcal{B}\) to basis \(\mathcal{C}\).
  • Standard Basis: The most common basis for a vector space, consisting of vectors with one component equal to 1 and all other components equal to 0.
  • Matrix Transpose: The matrix, denoted \(A^T\), formed by interchanging the rows and columns of the original matrix \(A\).

3. Formulas

  • Vector from Coordinates: \(\vec{v} = c_1\vec{b}_1 + c_2\vec{b}_2 + \dots + c_n\vec{b}_n\)
  • Change-of-Basis Transformation: \([\vec{v}]_{\mathcal{C}} = P_{\mathcal{C} \leftarrow \mathcal{B}} [\vec{v}]_{\mathcal{B}}\)
  • Change-of-Basis Matrix Composition: \(P_{\mathcal{C} \leftarrow \mathcal{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} [\vec{b}_1]_{\mathcal{C}} & [\vec{b}_2]_{\mathcal{C}} & \dots & [\vec{b}_n]_{\mathcal{C}} \end{bmatrix}\)
  • Change to Standard Basis Matrix: \(P_{\mathcal{S} \leftarrow \mathcal{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} \vec{b}_1 & \vec{b}_2 & \dots & \vec{b}_n \end{bmatrix}\)
  • Inverse Change-of-Basis: \(P_{\mathcal{B} \leftarrow \mathcal{C}} = (P_{\mathcal{C} \leftarrow \mathcal{B}})^{-1}\)
  • Double Transpose: \((A^T)^T = A\)
  • Transpose of a Sum: \((A + B)^T = A^T + B^T\)
  • Transpose of a Scalar Multiple: \((\lambda A)^T = \lambda A^T\)

4. Mistakes

  • Confusing the direction of the change-of-basis matrix: Using \(P_{\mathcal{C} \leftarrow \mathcal{B}}\) to convert from \(\mathcal{C}\) to \(\mathcal{B}\) coordinates. Why it’s wrong: The notation \(P_{\mathcal{C} \leftarrow \mathcal{B}}\) explicitly means “from \(\mathcal{B}\) to \(\mathcal{C}\).” For the reverse direction, the inverse matrix must be used.
  • Incorrectly constructing the change-of-basis matrix: Using the new basis vectors as columns instead of the coordinates of the old basis vectors. Why it’s wrong: The columns of \(P_{\mathcal{C} \leftarrow \mathcal{B}}\) must be the coordinates of the \(\mathcal{B}\) vectors relative to the \(\mathcal{C}\) basis, i.e., \([\vec{b}_i]_{\mathcal{C}}\).
  • Mixing up vectors and their coordinates: Treating a vector \(\vec{v}\) and its coordinate representation \([\vec{v}]_{\mathcal{B}}\) as the same thing. Why it’s wrong: A vector is a geometric object, while a coordinate vector is just a list of numbers that depends on the chosen basis.
  • Assuming a set of vectors is a basis without checking both conditions: A set of vectors might span a space but not be linearly independent, or vice versa. Why it’s wrong: A basis must satisfy both properties to uniquely define coordinates for every vector in the space.

5. Examples

5.1. Finding Standard Coordinates from a Custom Basis
Question: Consider the basis \(\mathcal{B} = \left\{ \vec{b}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}, \vec{b}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \right\}\) for \(\mathbb{R}^2\). The vector \(\vec{v}\) has coordinates \([\vec{v}]_{\mathcal{B}} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}\). What is \(\vec{v}\) in the standard coordinates, \([\vec{v}]_{\mathcal{S}}\)?
Click to see the solution
  1. Construct the change-of-basis matrix from \(\mathcal{B}\) to the standard basis \(\mathcal{S}\). The columns of this matrix are simply the vectors of basis \(\mathcal{B}\). \[ P_{\mathcal{S} \leftarrow \mathcal{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} \vec{b}_1 & \vec{b}_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \]
  2. Multiply the matrix by the coordinate vector \([\vec{v}]_{\mathcal{B}}\). \[ [\vec{v}]_{\mathcal{S}} = P_{\mathcal{S} \leftarrow \mathcal{B}} [\vec{v}]_{\mathcal{B}} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} \]
  3. Perform the matrix-vector multiplication. \[ [\vec{v}]_{\mathcal{S}} = \begin{pmatrix} (1)(2) + (3)(-1) \\ (2)(2) + (1)(-1) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 - 3 \\ 4 - 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix} \] Answer: The vector \(\vec{v}\) in standard coordinates is \(\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}\).
5.2. Finding Coordinates Relative to a Custom Basis
Question: Consider the basis \(\mathcal{C} = \left\{ \vec{c}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}, \vec{c}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} \right\}\). Find the coordinates of the vector \(\vec{v} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}\) relative to the basis \(\mathcal{C}\) (i.e., find \([\vec{v}]_{\mathcal{C}}\)).
Click to see the solution

We need to find scalars \(x\) and \(y\) such that \(x\vec{c}_1 + y\vec{c}_2 = \vec{v}\).

  1. Set up the vector equation. \[ x \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + y \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \]
  2. Translate this into a system of linear equations. \[ \begin{cases} 2x + y = 5 \\ x - y = 0 \end{cases} \]
  3. Solve the system. From the second equation, we get \(x = y\). Substituting this into the first equation: \[ 2x + (x) = 5 \implies 3x = 5 \implies x = \frac{5}{3} \] Since \(x = y\), we have \(y = \frac{5}{3}\).
  4. Write the coordinate vector. \[ [\vec{v}]_{\mathcal{C}} = \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 5/3 \\ 5/3 \end{pmatrix} \] Answer: The coordinate vector is \(\begin{pmatrix} 5/3 \\ 5/3 \end{pmatrix}\).
5.3. Finding the Change-of-Basis Matrix Between Two Bases
Question: Let \(\mathcal{B} = \left\{ \vec{b}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}, \vec{b}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} \right\}\) and \(\mathcal{C} = \left\{ \vec{c}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}, \vec{c}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \right\}\) be two bases for \(\mathbb{R}^2\). Find the change-of-basis matrix \(P_{\mathcal{C} \leftarrow \mathcal{B}}\).
Click to see the solution

We need to find the coordinates of the \(\mathcal{B}\) vectors relative to the \(\mathcal{C}\) basis. The columns of \(P_{\mathcal{C} \leftarrow \mathcal{B}}\) will be \([\vec{b}_1]_{\mathcal{C}}\) and \([\vec{b}_2]_{\mathcal{C}}\).

  1. Find \([\vec{b}_1]_{\mathcal{C}}\): Solve \(x_1\vec{c}_1 + x_2\vec{c}_2 = \vec{b}_1\). \[ x_1 \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + x_2 \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \implies \begin{cases} 2x_1 + x_2 = 1 \\ x_1 = 1 \end{cases} \] Solving gives \(x_1 = 1\) and \(x_2 = -1\). So, \([\vec{b}_1]_{\mathcal{C}} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}\).
  2. Find \([\vec{b}_2]_{\mathcal{C}}\): Solve \(y_1\vec{c}_1 + y_2\vec{c}_2 = \vec{b}_2\). \[ y_1 \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + y_2 \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} \implies \begin{cases} 2y_1 + y_2 = 1 \\ y_1 = -1 \end{cases} \] Solving gives \(y_1 = -1\) and \(y_2 = 3\). So, \([\vec{b}_2]_{\mathcal{C}} = \begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}\).
  3. Construct the matrix \(P_{\mathcal{C} \leftarrow \mathcal{B}}\). \[ P_{\mathcal{C} \leftarrow \mathcal{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} [\vec{b}_1]_{\mathcal{C}} & [\vec{b}_2]_{\mathcal{C}} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \] Answer: The change-of-basis matrix is \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\).
5.4. Applying a Change-of-Basis Matrix
Question: Using the bases from the previous example, let \([\vec{v}]_{\mathcal{B}} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}\). Find \([\vec{v}]_{\mathcal{C}}\) using the matrix \(P_{\mathcal{C} \leftarrow \mathcal{B}}\).
Click to see the solution
  1. Recall the change-of-basis matrix found in the previous problem. \[ P_{\mathcal{C} \leftarrow \mathcal{B}} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \]
  2. Apply the formula \([\vec{v}]_{\mathcal{C}} = P_{\mathcal{C} \leftarrow \mathcal{B}} [\vec{v}]_{\mathcal{B}}\). \[ [\vec{v}]_{\mathcal{C}} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \]
  3. Perform the matrix-vector multiplication. \[ [\vec{v}]_{\mathcal{C}} = \begin{pmatrix} (1)(3) + (-1)(1) \\ (-1)(3) + (3)(1) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 - 1 \\ -3 + 3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \] Answer: The coordinates of \(\vec{v}\) relative to basis \(\mathcal{C}\) are \(\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}\).
5.5. Coordinates in a Polynomial Space
Question: The set \(\mathcal{B} = \{1 - t^2, t - t^2, 2 - t + t^2\}\) is a basis for \(\mathbb{P}_2\) (the space of polynomials of degree \(\le 2\)). Find the coordinate vector of the polynomial \(p(t) = 3 + t - 6t^2\) relative to \(\mathcal{B}\).
Click to see the solution

We need to find scalars \(x, y, z\) such that \(x(1 - t^2) + y(t - t^2) + z(2 - t + t^2) = 3 + t - 6t^2\).

  1. Expand and group terms on the left side by powers of \(t\). \[ (x + 2z) + (y - z)t + (-x - y + z)t^2 = 3 + t - 6t^2 \]
  2. Equate the coefficients of corresponding powers of \(t\).
    • Constant terms: \(x + 2z = 3\)
    • Coefficients of \(t\): \(y - z = 1\)
    • Coefficients of \(t^2\): \(-x - y + z = -6\)
  3. Solve the system of linear equations.
    • From the second equation, \(y = 1 + z\).
    • Substitute \(y\) into the third equation: \(-x - (1+z) + z = -6 \implies -x - 1 = -6 \implies x = 5\).
    • Substitute \(x=5\) into the first equation: \(5 + 2z = 3 \implies 2z = -2 \implies z = -1\).
    • Substitute \(z=-1\) back into the equation for \(y\): \(y = 1 + (-1) = 0\).
  4. Form the coordinate vector. \[ [p]_{\mathcal{B}} = \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 0 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} \] Answer: The coordinate vector is \(\begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 0 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}\).
5.6. Calculating the Transpose of a Matrix
Question: Find the transpose of the matrix \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 5 \\ 1 & 9 \\ -3 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\).
Click to see the solution
  1. Identify the rows of matrix A.
    • Row 1: \([2, 5]\)
    • Row 2: \([1, 9]\)
    • Row 3: \([-3, 4]\)
  2. Make these rows the columns of the new matrix \(A^T\).
    • Column 1 of \(A^T\) is \([2, 1, -3]^T\).
    • Column 2 of \(A^T\) is \([5, 9, 4]^T\).
  3. Write the resulting matrix. \[ A^T = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & -3 \\ 5 & 9 & 4 \end{pmatrix} \] Answer: The transpose is \(\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & -3 \\ 5 & 9 & 4 \end{pmatrix}\).
5.7. Verifying the Transpose of a Sum Property
Question: Let \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\) and \(B = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & -1 \\ 2 & 5 \end{pmatrix}\). Show that \((A + B)^T = A^T + B^T\).
Click to see the solution
  1. Calculate the left side: \((A + B)^T\).
    • First, find the sum \(A+B\): \[ A+B = \begin{pmatrix} 1+4 & 3-1 \\ 2+2 & 0+5 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 4 & 5 \end{pmatrix} \]
    • Now, find the transpose of the sum: \[ (A+B)^T = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 4 \\ 2 & 5 \end{pmatrix} \]
  2. Calculate the right side: \(A^T + B^T\).
    • First, find the transposes \(A^T\) and \(B^T\): \[ A^T = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad B^T = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ -1 & 5 \end{pmatrix} \]
    • Now, add the transposes: \[ A^T + B^T = \begin{pmatrix} 1+4 & 2+2 \\ 3-1 & 0+5 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & 4 \\ 2 & 5 \end{pmatrix} \]
  3. Compare the results. The results from step 1 and step 2 are identical. Answer: Both sides of the equation result in the matrix \(\begin{pmatrix} 5 & 4 \\ 2 & 5 \end{pmatrix}\), verifying the property.
